content:
**Subject and central claims.** This section is Steven Pinker's evolutionary and cognitive account of humor and laughter, not a bibliography. He argues that laughter is a loud, involuntary broadcast rather than a release of psychic energy: its very costliness and unfakeability make it an honest advertisement of a mental state, produced by handing control from voluntary action systems to low-level bodily drivers (file page 316). He proposes two primate precursors — the mobbing call of collective aggression and the play signal marking mock aggression during tickling and rough-and-tumble play, where fighters must rehearse realistically yet signal "all in fun" (file page 316).

**Aggression, dignity, and status.** Humor often aggresses: being laughed at feels like an attack, and comedy runs on slapstick, insult, and Schadenfreude, illustrated by the Ye'Kwana laughing at an injured visitor and by Orwell's cinema audience (file pages 316–317). Yet cruelty alone is not the trigger; the target must possess an undeserved claim to dignity that humor punctures — hence the appeal of mocking the pompous, the powerful, and bodily pretension (sexual and scatological wit) (file page 317). Wit is also a rhetorical weapon: Reagan's one-liners and the "Yeah, yeah" double-affirmative joke show a quip can win a moment and seem to compress a truth (file page 317).

**Koestler's mechanism.** Pinker endorses Arthur Koestler's reverse-engineering: a train of thought in one frame meets an anomaly, resolved by shifting to a second frame in which the event makes sense and someone's dignity falls — the shift Koestler called "bisociation" (file page 318). The Churchill poison exchange, the mountain climber and God, and W. C. Fields's "clubs" pun each illustrate incongruity, resolution, and indignity (file page 318). Slapstick clashes a psychological frame (a person as locus of beliefs and desires) with a physical frame (matter obeying physics); scatological and sexual humor clash the psychological with physiological and biological frames; verbal humor clashes two meanings of one word (file page 318). Pinker explicitly rejects the rest of Koestler's theory — the hydraulic pressure model and an aggressive drive as the pressure source (file page 318).

**Three replacement ideas.** First, humor is an anti-dominance weapon: status is a beholder-weighted aura of prowess, skill, beauty, wealth and the like, and ridicule exposes any mortal's less-exalted qualities (file page 319). Second, dominance is enforceable one-on-one but fails before a coordinated mob; contagious, disruptive laughter lets scattered people simultaneously recognize the same infirmity in a target, as in "The Emperor's New Clothes" (file page 319). Third, a "principle of relevance" makes listeners charitably fill premises so words make sense — the Jane and the piggy bank passage shows inferred facts (child, coins, buying ice cream) never stated (file page 319). The jester hijacks this machinery so the audience deduces a disparaging proposition themselves; Reagan's abortion quip forces acceptance of a framing (born versus unborn) that a rebuttal would need many words to undo (file page 319).

**Limits and social bonding.** Not all humor is malicious: friendly banter and self-deprecation are common (file pages 319–320). Robert Provine's field observation found only ten to twenty percent of laughter episodes even indulgently humorous; typical laugh lines were "I'll see you guys later" (file page 320). Pinker's explanation: teasing deprecates qualities one could lord over a friend, signaling the relationship is friendship rather than dominance; laughter's involuntariness makes it hard to fake, and trial teases test whether ice is breaking (file page 320). The section closes by opening a new topic, "The Inquisitive in Pursuit of the Inconceivable," on supernatural belief (file page 320).

**Engineering implications (mine, not Pinker's).** For a thinking machine, this suggests mechanisms worth implementing: multiple frames or construals as data structures; anomaly detection when an event violates a frame's expectations; frame-switching that reinterprets the event; a dignity or status model tracking claims and their warrant; and a relevance-driven inference engine that fills unstated premises. A social layer could model signaling costs, coalition detection (shared laughter as coordination), and relationship typing (dominance versus friendship). None of this is demonstrated human intelligence or consciousness; the source supplies hypotheses and examples, not algorithms, and leaves unsolved how frames are represented, how the right second frame is selected, how warrant is computed, and how emotion, memory, and learning would ground these processes. The text is legible; the only uncertainty is the printed page labels, which appear as bracketed numbers (547–554) whose exact correspondence to file pages I cannot verify.
